questions.q: Stated precisely, what is the actual apples-to-apples speedup comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT?
options: The QFT and FFT have identical gate/operation counts, so there is no speedup
The comparison is meaningless because the FFT and QFT compute entirely different mathematical transforms

For transforming a vector of the same dimension N = 2^n, the QFT circuit uses O(n^2) quantum gates versus the FFT's O(n*2^n) classical operations -- an exponential improvement in n for building the same transform
The QFT is slower than the FFT in every possible case and offers no advantage at all
questions.explain: Both compute the same DFT matrix on a size-N vector; the QFT does it with O(n^2) quantum gates versus O(n*2^n) classical operations for the FFT -- a genuine exponential improvement in gate/operation count for the same-size transform.

questions.q: What happens when you measure a quantum register that has just had the QFT applied to it?
options: The register collapses to exactly one basis state, sampled according to probability (squared amplitude magnitude), and the information in every other amplitude is lost
You read out the complete list of all N output amplitudes simultaneously, just like a classical FFT's output array
The measurement has no effect on the quantum state at all
The register automatically re-runs the QFT circuit a second time before producing a result
questions.explain: A single measurement yields exactly one sampled basis state and destroys the rest of the superposition's amplitude information -- this is the readout problem that limits what the QFT's speedup actually buys you.

questions.q: Why is the readout problem described as 'the single most important honesty point' of this lesson, rather than a minor footnote?
options: Because it means the QFT can never be used for any practical purpose whatsoever

Because it defines exactly when the QFT's exponential gate-count advantage is actually usable: only when the surrounding algorithm needs one specific extractable piece of information, not the full output vector a classical FFT would hand you
Because it only applies to even values of n, not odd ones
Because it proves the QFT circuit construction from the previous lesson is mathematically incorrect
questions.explain: The readout problem is the scoping condition on the whole speedup claim: the QFT's exponential gate-count advantage is real, but it is only exploitable by algorithms specifically designed to need one extractable answer rather than a full classical-style printout.

questions.q: Why are quantum phase estimation and Shor's algorithm specifically structured around extracting a single number, rather than a full QFT output vector?
options: Because phase estimation and Shor's algorithm do not actually use the QFT at all
Because reading out a full vector from a quantum computer is actually cheap, so this design choice is purely stylistic
Because single-number extraction was historically easier to program, with no connection to the readout problem

Because they are engineered so the QFT step concentrates measurement probability onto basis states that reveal exactly one needed value (a phase, or a period) using few measurements -- sidestepping the readout problem entirely
questions.explain: Both algorithms are deliberately designed so the needed answer is concentrated onto one (or a few) basis states by the QFT step, so a small number of measurements suffice -- this is exactly how they avoid needing the full, unreadable output vector.

questions.q: A classmate claims: 'Since the QFT needs only O(n^2) gates versus the FFT's O(n*2^n) operations, you should always use a quantum computer instead of a classical one whenever you need to Fourier-transform data.' What is the flaw in this claim?
options: It ignores the readout problem: if the goal requires the full, explicit output vector as classical data, the QFT does not help, because you cannot cheaply read out all N amplitudes -- you would need to re-run and re-measure repeatedly, eroding the gate-count advantage
The flaw is that the QFT can only be applied to real numbers, never complex ones
The flaw is that O(n^2) is actually larger than O(n*2^n) for all values of n
There is no flaw; the claim is entirely correct and quantum computers should replace all classical FFT use
questions.explain: The gate-count advantage only matters if you don't need the full output vector. If the task genuinely requires reading out every amplitude as explicit classical data, the quantum approach loses its advantage because full readout requires repeated runs and measurements.
